finding: Test 19 asserts "a cap set to an equal or lower value exits 0" without qualification, but §5.1 now carves out an exception: for `run_max_budget_usd` and `run_max_unit_budget_usd` the value 0 means *disabled*, so setting either to 0 is a raise and is refused. An engineer writing test 19 from its own text picks 0 as the obvious "lower" value for a budget field and asserts exit 0; an engineer writing it from §5.1 asserts exit 2. Two contradictory tests from one requirement.
suggestion: Rewrite test 19's middle clause as: "a cap set to an equal or lower non-zero value exits 0, and setting either budget field to 0 exits 2 as a raise", so the test carries §5.1's exception rather than contradicting it.

finding: Test 26 asserts the Stop hook "does block one that ended with neither its durable write nor a record", speaking of "a unit" generally. §6.2 scopes the Stop hook to `review-role` and `audit-role` only — it "fires when `TP_UNIT_KIND` ends in `-role`" — and explicitly leaves every other kind's predicate to the driver. An `implement` unit that ends with its task still `wip` and no escalation record must NOT be blocked, so test 26 as written fails on the very case its wording invites.
suggestion: Scope test 26 to role units and add the negative: "the Stop hook blocks a role unit that ended with neither its findings file nor a record, does not block one that wrote an escalation record, and does not fire at all for a non-role kind."

finding: An `audit-fix` unit's id is the finding's `role:item_id` (§3.1), but the command the kind must run is `tp audit --resolve <results.ndjson> <idx> …` — a 0-based index into `$TP_ROUND_DIR/merged.ndjson`. The spec never says how the unit converts its id into that index, nor how the driver evaluates the durable write ("That row carries a disposition") — that also requires locating a row by role+item_id and knowing that the pair is unique in the merged file. An implementer must invent both the lookup and the uniqueness assumption, and a wrong index disposes some other finding.
suggestion: Either state that `merged.ndjson` rows carry a stable `role`+`item_id` pair that is unique within a round and that both the unit and the driver locate the row by that pair (defining what happens when it is absent or duplicated), or make the unit id the index itself and record `role:item_id` as a separate display field.

finding: Round 10 named the audit results file `$TP_ROUND_DIR/merged.ndjson`, placing the record unit's OUTPUT inside the directory §6.3 defines as the record unit's INPUT glob (`the review-record and audit-record units merge $TP_ROUND_DIR/*.ndjson, which holds exactly their own round's files`). A retried or re-run `audit-record` unit — which §3.1 explicitly plans for, since `TP_ROUND_DIR` is keyed by the cycle so a round survives a driver death — would re-merge merged.ndjson into itself and double-count every row, and §6.3's claim that the directory holds exactly the round's role files is now false. It also collides with §3.1's rule that a round directory holds at most one file per role and with §4.1's role-skipping scan of that directory, which would see a pseudo-role named `merged`.
suggestion: Put the merged file outside the role-file glob — e.g. `$TP_ROUND_DIR/merged/results.ndjson` or `.tp/rounds/<base>/<phase>-r$TP_ROUND-merged.ndjson` — or state in §6.3 that the merge input is `$TP_ROUND_DIR/*.ndjson` excluding `merged.ndjson`, and say that a re-run record unit overwrites rather than accumulates.

finding: `audit-fix` now depends on `$TP_ROUND_DIR/merged.ndjson` existing (round 10's naming repair), but `audit-record`'s durable-write column is still only `An audit round file for $TP_ROUND exists`. An `audit-record` unit can therefore exit 0 and pass the driver's success test with merged.ndjson absent, after which every `audit-fix` unit in that round has no file to pass to `tp audit --resolve` and no way to satisfy its own predicate (`That row carries a disposition in the round's results file`). The dependency was introduced without extending the producing kind's predicate.
suggestion: Extend `audit-record`'s durable write to `An audit round file for $TP_ROUND exists and $TP_ROUND_DIR/merged.ndjson is present and wholly parseable`, and add a test asserting an `audit-record` that records the round without writing the results file is a failed attempt.

finding: The run-state schema in §3.5 has no `phase` field (only run_id, started_at, stop_reason, totals, units[]), yet the same section requires `tp run --status` to print "phase" for the current or last run and to carry `spec_coverage_clean_rounds`, `role_streaks` and `divergence` "on a stop in the audit phase". For a stopped run the driver has no recorded phase to gate that on: re-deriving it from `tp resume` reports the phase now, not the phase at the stop, and inferring it from the last unit's `kind` is nowhere stated. §1 hangs its central promise (the operator gets the divergence signals at the end of a run) on this conditional, and test 14 asserts it.
suggestion: Add `phase` (and, if the audit branch is round-scoped, `round`) to the run-state object written at stop time, and say in §3.5 that --status reads the audit branch off that recorded phase — or state explicitly that the phase is derived from the last unit row's kind prefix.

finding: The two budget fences are unresolvable at their own defaults. §7 defaults `run_max_budget_usd` and `run_max_unit_budget_usd` to 0, and §5.1 says both "an equal ... value is accepted and exits 0" and "setting either to 0 is a raise and is refused". On a repo that has not overridden them — the default case — `tp set --workflow run_max_budget_usd=0` is simultaneously equal (accept) and a raise (refuse). No deterministic test can be written for the most common configuration.
suggestion: State which rule wins when the resolved value is already 0 — e.g. "0 is refused only when the resolved value is non-zero; a no-op 0-to-0 set is accepted", or refuse 0 unconditionally and drop the equal-value acceptance for the two budget fields.

finding: The emitted findings path is pinned to `$TP_ROUND_DIR/$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson`, but `tp review`/`tp audit` emit one output filename per active role in a single invocation, and `TP_UNIT_ID` is a single value that is the round number inside a `review-record`/`audit-record` unit (§3.1). Under `TP_ROUND_DIR` the rule therefore yields either N identical paths for N roles, or `$TP_ROUND_DIR/<round>.ndjson` in a record unit. Test 27 ("tp review and tp audit emit the round-scoped findings path") has no single expected string to assert.
suggestion: Define the emitted path by the role being prompted, not by the unit: `$TP_ROUND_DIR/<role_id>.ndjson`, and note that in a role unit `TP_UNIT_ID` equals that role id. Then state what a record unit's invocation emits (or that it emits nothing).

finding: §6.3 has the `review-record` and `audit-record` units merge `$TP_ROUND_DIR/*.ndjson`, while §3.3 places the audit round's merged output at `$TP_ROUND_DIR/merged.ndjson` — inside the glob it is the product of. §3.1 deliberately keeps `TP_ROUND_DIR` keyed by the cycle rather than the run so a round survives a driver death, and §3.1 only deletes the *role* files of units the oracle returns; nothing deletes `merged.ndjson`. A second record unit for the same round (driver death, or a re-run role forcing a re-record) therefore merges its own previous output back in alongside the role files, double-counting every row that survived the first merge — and, for the audit side, re-ingesting rows that `audit-fix` units have already disposed.
suggestion: Either place the merged output outside the glob (e.g. `$TP_ROUND_DIR/../<phase>-r$TP_ROUND-merged.ndjson`, or a `merged/` subdirectory) or specify the merge input as the per-role files by name (`$TP_ROUND_DIR/<role>.ndjson` for the phase's active roles) and state that the record unit truncates any prior merged file before writing.

finding: §6.3 says `tp-reviewer` and `tp-auditor` "may write exactly one path — their own findings file at `$TP_ROUND_DIR/$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson` — and are denied every other write", with no carve-out for writes made through tp's own CLI. §5.2 makes escalation a normal outcome for any unit and requires the unit to run `tp escalate`, which writes `$TP_RUN_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-escalation.json`; §6.2's Stop hook is specified to check for exactly that record inside a role unit, and test 26 asserts a role unit that wrote one is not blocked. Under the literal §6.3 restriction a role unit can never produce that record. §6.2 states the shell carve-out for the PreToolUse matcher ("Shell tools are deliberately outside the matcher"); §6.3 states no equivalent, so the two fences read as governing different sets.
suggestion: State in §6.3 that the write restriction covers file-writing tools only and that tp commands invoked through the shell (notably `tp escalate`) are outside it — mirroring §6.2's wording — or add the escalation path to the reviewer/auditor allowlist explicitly.

finding: Test 15 enumerates exactly four git-ignored paths and §10.7 confirms "The `.tp/.gitignore` fixture gains four entries", but §3.1 introduces a fifth new path under `.tp/` — the run lock at `.tp/locks/run-<base>.lock` — whose ignore status the spec never states. A test writer following §10.7 asserts a four-entry fixture and a lock file then shows up untracked-or-committed depending on what the existing fixture already covers.
suggestion: Say whether `.tp/locks/` is git-ignored, and make the count in test 15 and §10.7 agree with the answer (five entries if it is).

finding: Test 16 requires that "Each §7 field takes its documented default, accepts both range endpoints, and rejects one step outside each", but two of the seven §7 fields have no endpoints (`runner`: "Built-in name or object"; `notify_cmd`: "Any command string"), and "one step" is undefined for the three decimal-dollar fields — one engineer rejects `-1`/`10001`, another `-0.01`/`10000.01`, and a third asks whether `run_max_budget_usd=0.005` is in range at all.
suggestion: Restrict test 16's endpoint clause to the five numeric fields, state the rejection probes explicitly (e.g. "one below the low endpoint and one above the high endpoint, using 0.01 for decimal fields"), and pin the accepted precision for the dollar fields.

finding: Test 31 requires exit 2 "for every command, including cobra's own built-ins", but §8a.5 only requires that "Every command's `Args` validator exits 2" plus the already-2 unknown-command case. Cobra-generated commands (`help`, `completion`) are not tp commands with tp-authored `Args` validators, and the section never claims they are covered, so the test asserts a requirement no section states — and its fix (overriding cobra's built-ins) is a different change from the one §8a.5 describes.
suggestion: Either extend §8a.5 to say the arity behaviour applies to cobra's generated commands as well and how (a root-level `Args`/error handler override), or drop "including cobra's own built-ins" from test 31 and scope it to tp-defined commands.

finding: Test 40 asserts `runner` and `notify_cmd` "cannot be set at any layer" under `TP_UNATTENDED=1`, mirroring §5.1's "a unit cannot set them at all, at any layer". Two readings produce opposite tests: (a) every `tp set --workflow runner=...`/`notify_cmd=...` write exits 2 whatever layer it targets, values already resolved from config still apply; (b) the fields are additionally ignored during resolution under the variable — which would strip the operator's own configured runner from the driver. The section never says which, and the difference is observable.
suggestion: State explicitly that the fence refuses writes only, and that values already present in `.tp/config.json`/`.tp/local.json` continue to resolve normally under the variable; then reword test 40 as "every attempt to write `runner` or `notify_cmd` exits 2 regardless of target layer, while an already-configured value still resolves".

finding: §10.7 says "The `.tp/.gitignore` fixture gains four entries" and test 15 names exactly four paths (`.tp/run-<base>.json`, `.tp/runs/`, `.tp/rounds/`, `.tp/last_failure-<base>.json`). §3.1 introduces a fifth new artifact under `.tp/`: the run lock at `.tp/locks/run-<base>.lock`, described as "a distinct run-scoped lock", i.e. a path the repo does not already carry. Nothing ignores it, so an unattended run leaves a lock file in the working tree — which also collides with the release rule that a task close must leave a clean tree.
suggestion: Add `.tp/locks/` to the gitignore entries and update §10.7's count and test 15's list to five, or state that `.tp/locks/` is already covered by an existing entry.

finding: Removing the present-only predicate left the deletion rule over-broad: `the driver then deletes the file of every unit that set does contain, immediately before spawning it`. Only the two `-role` kinds have such a file; the other six have no findings file at all, and for `implement` the durable write is a task status, so `deletes the file of every unit` is undefined or destructive when read literally. Test 45 repeats the same over-generalization (`deletes the file of every unit the oracle did return`), while test 17 gets it right (`its role findings file is deleted before the attempt`).
suggestion: Scope both the §3.1 sentence and test 45 to role units: `the driver then deletes the findings file of every role unit in that set, immediately before spawning it; other kinds have no such file`.

finding: `runner` "takes one of three shapes: a built-in template name, a runner object, or a map from unit kind to either of those with a `default` key". A runner object and a per-kind map are both JSON objects, and the spec gives no rule for telling them apart — an object with a `default` key could be either. The only stated error is "a map missing `default` is a usage error", which presupposes the classification the implementer has to invent, and a misclassified object either silently loses the per-kind routing or reports a spurious usage error.
suggestion: Pin the discriminator explicitly: e.g. an object carrying `cmd` is a runner object, any other object is a per-kind map (whose keys must be the eight §3.3 kinds plus `default`), and an object carrying both `cmd` and unit-kind keys is a usage error with its own hint.

finding: §3.2.2 defines spend only for the success path and for a runner that declares no `spend_key`. It says nothing about a runner that declares one where the final log line is missing, is not JSON, lacks the dot path, or holds a non-numeric value. That is the common case for a crashed or budget-killed child, and every option an implementer could pick (spend null and continue, treat as 0, fail the unit, exit 2) changes when `cap-budget` trips.
suggestion: State the rule for an unreadable spend key — recommended: the unit's `spend_usd` is null, the run's accrued total is unchanged, and the condition is reported once in `--status` rather than failing the unit — and say whether a null spend on a metered runner is distinguishable from an unmetered runner's null.

finding: Round 10 made test 5 assert concurrency `from the seam's recorded spawn and exit timestamps`, but §3.2.1's `TP_RUNNER_SEAM` contract was not extended: it specifies the seam's `cmd`, its four positional args, its `spend_key`, and one final log line carrying the cost key — no timestamp recording. Test 1 likewise only says the seam `records every invocation and returns scripted exit codes`. The run state (§3.5) records `duration_seconds` but no spawn instant, so nothing the spec defines can establish that two role units overlapped. The assertion has no specified mechanism behind it.
suggestion: State in §3.2.1 that the seam records, per invocation, the unit kind, id, attempt and the spawn and exit timestamps to a seam-owned file, and name that file so test 5 and test 1 read the same artifact.

finding: `decompose`'s durable write is "The task file holds at least one task" — a condition that is already true whenever the task file is non-empty. After an attempt that imports tasks and then exits non-zero, the retry's predicate is satisfied before the retry starts, so a no-op retry that exits 0 is scored a success. §3.3 claims every predicate is "a state, never a delta" and test 18 asserts only that each is decidable from one file, so nothing in §10 can distinguish a decompose that did the work from one that did nothing.
suggestion: Either tighten the predicate to something the unit must newly establish (e.g. "every task the phase requires is present and `tp validate` reports no coverage gap") or state plainly that `decompose` runs only against an empty task file and add a test that a retry after a partial import is still required to complete the import.

finding: "A unit is attempted `1 + run_max_unit_retries` times" never says when the retry happens or where the attempt count lives. Retrying inside the same iteration and retrying by letting the next iteration re-select the same unit are different implementations with different observable behaviour (caps are evaluated between iterations only, §3.4), and the second needs a persistent attempt counter — which §3.5 forbids reading back from the run state, so the count would have to be re-derived from the run's in-memory history. For a batch of concurrent role units it is also unstated whether a failed sibling is retried while the others are still in flight.
suggestion: State that retries are performed inside the same iteration, immediately after the failed attempt (and, for a concurrent batch, after the whole batch has exited), that the attempt counter is per `(kind, id)` and in-memory for the life of the run, and that a new `tp run` starts every unit's attempt count at 1.

finding: Round 10's exit-code definition — `tp run exits 0 on converged, 4 on every other stop_reason, and 2 on a usage error before the loop starts`, with `stop_reason names which of the seven it was` — contradicts §3.1's unchanged rule that a second concurrent `tp run` over the same task file `exits 4`. That failure happens before the loop starts and produces no `stop_reason` (there is no `lock-held` row in the table), so exit 4 no longer implies a recorded reason, and §8a.5's uniformity claim that exit 2 means `tp did not run the request` fails for the one case where tp most clearly did not run it.
suggestion: Pick one: either make the lock conflict a usage error (exit 2, consistent with §8a.5), or add a `lock-held` row to the stop_reason table so every exit 4 still names its reason, and correct the count in §3.4's sentence accordingly.

finding: Log paths are `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl`, and §3.1 makes an `audit-fix` unit's id the finding's `role:item_id` — a value that routinely contains `:` and can contain `/`, `§` or whitespace, since `item_id` is authored by a role. No sanitisation rule is given, so test 17 ("a retried unit gets a fresh log path") and any assertion over a log filename cannot state an expected string for the `audit-fix` kind, and a `/` in `item_id` silently redirects the log into a subdirectory.
suggestion: Pin a filename-safe transform for the `<id>` component (e.g. replace every character outside `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` with `-`, truncating at N chars) and say the unit's canonical `id` in the run state stays unmangled, so the two are separately assertable.

finding: Two sections give the unit log two different owners. §3.5 says "Each unit's runner output streams to `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl`", i.e. the driver captures the child's stdout; §3.2.1 defines the test seam's args as `["{unit_kind}","{unit_id}","{log_path}","{max_budget_usd}"]` and says "The fake runner writes a final log line carrying that key", i.e. the child writes the file at `{log_path}` itself, and `{log_path}` is a first-class placeholder in §3.2's table for any runner. If both happen the driver's redirect and the child's own writes race on one path and the final line the spend read depends on (§3.2.2) is not well defined.
suggestion: State once who owns the file: either the driver always redirects the child's stdout to the log path and `{log_path}` is informational only (say so), or a runner that consumes `{log_path}` writes it and the driver does not redirect — and say which rule the seam follows.

finding: `last_failure` has two triggers — "a unit exits non-zero, or closes with a failed quality gate" — but only the first is pinned to a writer and a context. Nothing says which process writes the gate-failure record (the driver, which sees only an exit code, or the child's own `tp done`), whether a gate failure that the unit then recovers from still leaves a record, or what `unit_kind`/`unit_id`/`phase` hold when `tp done` fails a gate outside a run with no `TP_UNIT_*` set. Test 23 exercises only the non-zero-exit path, so the second trigger is unasserted and unwritable.
suggestion: State that `tp done` writes `last_failure` on a gate failure only when `TP_UNIT_KIND`/`TP_UNIT_ID` are present (no record outside a run), and add a test asserting the record's fields after a gate-failed close inside a unit.

finding: `last_failure` has two writers with different knowledge. The non-zero-exit case is the driver's, which knows `(unit_kind, unit_id)`; the "closes with a failed quality gate" case happens inside a child `tp done`, which can only learn those from `TP_UNIT_KIND`/`TP_UNIT_ID`. The spec never says whether `tp done` writes the file outside a run (where both are unset, so the `(unit_kind, unit_id)` clearing key has no value), nor which component clears it on success — the driver after a successful unit, or the child's own successful `tp` command.
suggestion: Name the writer and clearer per case: the driver writes and clears on unit boundaries using `(unit_kind, unit_id)`; a gate failure inside a child writes only when `TP_UNIT_KIND` and `TP_UNIT_ID` are both set, and is a no-op outside a run. State the same for clearing so no path writes a record with an unmatched key.

finding: The round-10 budget-cap repair contradicts the rule immediately preceding it. §5.1 says `an equal or lower value is accepted and exits 0`, then says `setting either to 0 is a raise and is refused` — unconditionally. Both budget fields default to 0 (§7), so under the default resolution a unit setting `run_max_budget_usd=0` or `run_max_unit_budget_usd=0` is simultaneously an equal value (accept) and a raise (refuse). Test 19 was not realigned with the repair: it still asserts `a cap set to an equal or lower value exits 0`, which now has a counterexample the spec cannot decide.
suggestion: Scope the exception to the transition rather than the value: refuse only when the resolved value is non-zero and the requested value is 0; setting 0 when the resolved value is already 0 is a no-op and exits 0. Update test 19 to name both the accepted 0→0 case and the refused non-zero→0 case.

finding: `tp escalate --decision` accepts `skip-gate`, `raise-review-cap`, `raise-audit-cap`, `import-force` or `other` — a mirror of §5.1's fence table, except that §5.1 has a fourth refusal row (`tp set --workflow run_max_*=` above the resolved value) plus the stricter `runner`/`notify_cmd` fence, and neither has a `decision` value. Every driver-cap escalation therefore lands in `other`, which is the one value that tells the operator nothing about which decision is being asked for — in a payload whose whole purpose is to name the decision.
suggestion: Add a `raise-run-cap` value (and decide whether `runner`/`notify_cmd` warrant one, or belong to `other` by design), and state in §5.2 that the enum tracks §5.1's table row for row.

finding: The preflight minimum is given twice with different values: "if `tp` is absent from `PATH` or older than `0.35.0`" and "The minimum is `plugin.json`'s own version, compared against `tp --version`". These agree only while plugin.json reads 0.35.0. Test 50 ("below the plugin's minimum version") therefore has two candidate fixtures — a hard-coded 0.34.x boundary or a synthetic plugin.json version — and the two diverge the moment the plugin is versioned ahead of the binary.
suggestion: Keep one definition. Say the minimum is `plugin.json`'s `version` field, cite 0.35.0 only as its value at release, and have test 50 drive the boundary from a fixture plugin.json rather than a literal.

finding: The Stop hook must apply §3.3's predicate — file present *and every line parses as JSON* — plus a schema-valid check on the escalation record, within a 10-second timeout (§6.4), but the spec never says what the shipped hooks are written in or what they may depend on. "The predicate is two conditions over one file precisely so a hook can implement it without tp's state readers" still requires an NDJSON parser, which POSIX shell does not have; picking `jq`, `python3`, or a `tp` subcommand is a hard dependency choice the implementer would have to make unilaterally, and each choice changes the plugin's portability and the §6.1 preflight.
suggestion: State the hook implementation language and its allowed dependencies (e.g. POSIX shell calling `tp` only, with a `tp run --check-role-file <path>` style helper for the predicate), so hook, oracle and driver share one parser and test 52's three-way agreement is structural rather than three re-implementations.

finding: "When `TP_ROUND_DIR` is set, `tp review` and `tp audit` emit that same path as the role's output file" — the path being `$TP_ROUND_DIR/$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson`. But a single `tp review`/`tp audit` invocation emits prompts for every active role, and `TP_UNIT_ID` names exactly one role, so under the driver every emitted prompt would name the same output file. It is also undefined what these commands emit when `TP_ROUND_DIR` is set but `TP_UNIT_ID` is not (an interactive session inside a round directory).
suggestion: Derive the emitted path from the role the prompt is for — `$TP_ROUND_DIR/<role-id>.ndjson` — and say that `TP_UNIT_ID` is not consulted, so a multi-role invocation emits one distinct path per role and a single-role unit gets the same path the driver and the Stop hook check.

finding: §7 states `notify_cmd` is "per-operator rather than per-project and is read from `.tp/local.json` only", then states that `tp config --resolved`, `tp config --extract` and `tp validate --project` cover the new fields "on the same terms as every existing workflow field". `--extract` writes workflow values into the committed `.tp/config.json` and `--project` validates that file; applied uniformly they would both write and bless a `notify_cmd` in a layer §7 has just declared unreadable for that field. Test 16 pins the local-only rule but not the interaction with the three commands.
suggestion: Carve `notify_cmd` out of `--extract` (never extracted) and say what `--resolved` reports for it and what `validate --project` does when it finds a `notify_cmd` in `.tp/config.json` — rejecting it, or warning that it is ignored.

finding: `location_clusters` is added to `tp review --merge`'s payload, which already carries every merged record with its `location`, `role` and `severity` — so on the merge side the block is fully derivable from bytes in the same payload, and §8a.1 states it feeds no arithmetic, no `clean` flag and no exit code. §7 specifies `--compact` treatment for the run-state payload only, so the spec adds three new blocks to agent-facing outputs (`location_clusters`, `inputs` in §8a.4, `file_summary.truncated`/`total_changed` in §8a.3) without saying which survive `--compact`. Under P3 the merge-side cluster block is the one that pays for nothing an agent cannot re-derive.
suggestion: State the `--compact` rule for the new blocks in §8a (or as a line in §7 alongside the run-status rule): `location_clusters` is stripped under `--compact` on `--merge`, where the records it summarizes are present, and retained on `--status`, where they are not; `inputs` and the `file_summary` flags survive because they carry facts no other key holds. Add the assertion to test 28 so the compact contract is measured rather than assumed.

finding: §8a.4's rule is whole-file: `--merge` exits 1 only when an input has content lines and *none* parsed. §3.3's role predicate is stricter — "exists and every line parses" — and §6.2/test 52 pin the oracle, driver and Stop hook to that stricter form. So the codebase carries two definitions of a usable role file, and the merge keeps exactly the defect §8a.4 was written to remove at smaller granularity: a file where 12 of 13 lines parse still exits 0, still undercounts, and `--record` still freezes the round. The section's own rationale — "an unattended driver reads the exit code alone" — applies unchanged to the partial case, and outside a run (a hand-invoked `--merge`) the role predicate does not protect it.
suggestion: Either align the merge with §3.3 (any skipped content line in an input makes `--merge` exit 1) or state explicitly why the partial case is left at exit 0, naming the role predicate as the compensating control and the manual-merge case as accepted.

finding: §8a.5 fixes exit 2 to mean uniformly "tp did not run the request", yet §5.2 has a *successful* `tp escalate` — which ran the request and wrote its record — exit 2, and an escalate outside a run (a genuine usage error) exit 2 as well. Test 22 asks for both behaviours in one line ("writes the per-unit record and exits 2 ... outside a run it is a usage error") with no observable that separates them, so the usage-error half is only assertable via the record's absence, which the test does not say.
suggestion: Add to §8a.5 that `tp escalate` is the one deliberate exception to the exit-2 meaning (the record is the signal, §5.2), and reword test 22's last clause as "outside a run it exits 2 and writes no record".

finding: The round-10 realignment moved tests into §10.5 but left tests 33–40 under a heading that does not own them. §10.5 `Signals the driver reads` maps to §8a's five subsections, which tests 28–32 already cover one-for-one. Tests 33–34 are §3.4 caps and precedence, 35–37 are §3.1/§3.5 run state and environment, 38 is §4.1's oracle contract, 39 is §6.2's Stop hook, and 40 is §5.1's fencing — i.e. §10.1, §10.2 and §10.4 material. The same misfiling the repair set out to remove survives for eight of the section's thirteen tests.
suggestion: Move 33–34 and 37 to §10.1, 35–36 to §10.2, 38 to §10.1 (or a §10.2 oracle group), 39 to §10.4, and 40 to §10.3, leaving §10.5 as 28–32 plus any further §8a assertions.

finding: Test 40 (line 671) is immediately followed by the `### 10.6 Invariants across components` heading on line 672 with no intervening blank line — the only heading in the spec without one, and adjacent to the test lines round 10 moved. Every other §10 subsection heading is preceded by a blank line.
suggestion: Insert a blank line before `### 10.6`.

finding: Test 43's second clause — every shipped hook "exits non-zero rather than hanging" — names no observable. §6.4 fixes the declared `timeout` at 10 seconds, which is assertable from the hook manifest, but "rather than hanging" describes behaviour under a condition the test never constructs, and no fixture or expected exit code is given.
suggestion: Split it: assert the declared 10-second timeout from each hook's manifest entry, and assert the runtime half against a fixture that forces the slow path (e.g. a stubbed `tp` that sleeps past the timeout) with the expected non-zero code named.

finding: "the driver then deletes the file of every unit that set does contain, immediately before spawning it" is written over every unit, but only role units have a file at a driver-known path. For `implement`, `review-record`, `review-resolve`, `decompose`, `audit-record` and `audit-fix` there is no such file, so the sentence has no defined referent and an implementer must guess that it is role-only (test 45 repeats the same over-broad wording).
suggestion: Scope the sentence to role units: "for every `review-role`/`audit-role` unit the oracle returned, the driver deletes `$TP_ROUND_DIR/<role>.ndjson` immediately before spawning it; other kinds have no pre-spawn deletion" — and mirror that wording in test 45.

finding: The paragraph edited in round 10 ends `Without it the kind has no way to record the no-code-change outcome §3.3 admits` — a section citing itself. The reference reads as pointing elsewhere and gives a reader no target; it is a leftover from the sentence having been written for a different section.
suggestion: Replace with an in-section pointer: `the no-code-change outcome the table above admits`.

finding: §3.4 says "Caps are evaluated between iterations only. Children already spawned run to completion, so a run can overshoot its wall-clock and budget caps by at most one iteration" — naming two of the three quantitative caps. `run_max_units` overshoots on the same terms: one iteration spawns every role unit of a phase concurrently (§3.3), so the attempt count can pass the cap by up to (active roles − 1) before the between-iteration check sees it. The table row reads as a hard bound ("Spawned children reached `run_max_units`"), and test 33 pins three counters to the same number without pinning the bound.
suggestion: Extend the overshoot sentence to `run_max_units` and state the bound (one iteration's worth of concurrent units), or evaluate the unit cap at spawn time and say so.

finding: The log path is `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl`, and a unit's `id` is a task id, a role id, a round number, a spec base name, or the `role:item_id` of an audit finding (§3.1). The last form embeds a colon, and neither `item_id` nor a task id is stated to be free of path separators, so the spec gives no sanitization or escaping rule for turning a unit id into a filename.
suggestion: State the mapping from unit id to path component — either a documented sanitization (replace every character outside `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` with `-`) or use `seq` alone plus `kind` in the filename and keep the full id in the run-state row.
